lead: Phase equilibria answers one question: when two phases sit together and nothing changes any more, what must be true? This unit builds the answer from the chemical potential, counts the variables you are free to fix, and then turns the result into working equations for vapour-liquid, high-pressure, liquid-liquid and solid-liquid systems. After it you can compute a bubble or dew point, decode a P-x-y diagram, use Raoult, Henry and fugacity coefficients in the right pressure range, and get a solubility from a heat of fusion.
about: Unit 6 answers one question: when two phases sit together without changing, what must be true? Chapter 6.1 derives the answer — equal temperature, equal pressure and equal chemical potential (fugacity) of every component — and adds the stability test that decides whether one phase or two will form. Chapter 6.2 counts variables against equations to get the phase rule and Duhem's theorem, the tools that say which variables you may fix. Chapter 6.3 applies the equality to a pure substance, giving the vapour-pressure curve and the P-x-y diagram. Chapter 6.4 turns this into Raoult's law and its activity-coefficient correction; 6.5 covers the dilute limit through Henry's law; 6.6 swaps activity coefficients for fugacity coefficients at high pressure. Chapter 6.7 handles liquid-liquid and solid-liquid equilibria.

chapters.idea: At equilibrium every phase shares the same T and P, and every component has the same chemical potential (same fugacity) in every phase; a phase survives only if its Gibbs energy is a minimum, not a saddle.
chapters.depth: Start from dG = −S dT + V dP + Σ μ_i dn_i for a system of C components. Define μ_i, the chemical potential, also called the partial molar Gibbs energy, in J/mol. At fixed T and P with no reaction, equilibrium needs μ_i^α = μ_i^β for every component i and every pair of phases α and β. Convert to fugacity f_i (Pa) because μ carries an arbitrary reference value: μ_i = μ_i° + RT ln(f_i/f_i°), so the rule becomes f_i^α = f_i^β. State the other two conditions: thermal (T^α = T^β) and mechanical (P^α = P^β), and note why a curved interface can hold a small pressure jump. Then stability: at fixed T and P, G must rise for any small change of composition, so (∂²G/∂x₁²)_{T,P} > 0. Define the spinodal (second derivative zero), the binodal (common tangent) and the unstable gap between them. Some syllabi word the first half as 'criterion of equilibrium' and the second as 'criterion of stability'.

figure.title: Gibbs energy of mixing and the unstable region
figure.aria: Plot of molar Gibbs energy of mixing against x₁ for A = 0, 1.5 and 2.5; the A = 2.5 curve rises in the middle, so a mixture near x₁ = 0.5 lowers its energy by splitting into two phases.

chapters.example: At 300 K and 1 bar, the molar Gibbs energy of mixing of a binary liquid is given by g^M/RT = x₁ ln x₁ + x₂ ln x₂ + A x₁x₂ with A = 2.5. Test the equimolar mixture (x₁ = 0.5) for stability.
chapters.trap: Equating partial pressures instead of fugacities, and calling a mixture stable because the first derivative of G is zero — the second derivative must be positive too.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 (Gibbs energy, fundamental relations) and Unit 5 (chemical potential, fugacity).
chapters.leave: Maxwell relations and residual-property algebra stay in Unit 4; activity coefficient models stay in Unit 5.

chapters.idea: F = C − P + 2 counts the intensive variables you may set freely, and Duhem's theorem says that in a closed system of known overall composition two variables fix everything.
chapters.depth: Define phase (P), component (C) and degree of freedom (F). Derive the rule by counting: unknowns are T, P and C − 1 mole fractions per phase, giving 2 + P(C − 1); relations are the C(P − 1) chemical-potential equalities; subtraction gives F = C − P + 2. Handle reacting systems: C = number of species − number of independent reactions − any other constraint such as electroneutrality. Show the reduced rule F = C − P + 1 when T or P is held fixed, the everyday case of a hood at 1 atm. Then Duhem's theorem: in a closed system whose overall composition is known, fixing any two independent intensive variables fixes all remaining intensive variables and the amounts of every phase. Give the count as a one-line argument. Worked consequence: a binary VLE point fixed by T and x₁ has P and y₁ determined, which is why a P-x-y diagram is a pair of curves and not a surface.

figure.title: Counting degrees of freedom
figure.aria: Flow of the phase-rule count from unknowns to equations to F = C − P + 2, then to Duhem's theorem and the binary VLE case.

chapters.example: Find F for each case. (a) Pure water with liquid and vapour present. (b) Ethanol–water liquid and vapour at a fixed total pressure of 1 atm. (c) A gas of N₂, H₂ and NH₃ at 1 atm in which NH₃ ⇌ ½N₂ + 3/2H₂ can occur.
chapters.trap: Counting species as components when a reaction exists, and adding the full +2 when the pressure is already fixed.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 for the equilibrium equations being counted.
chapters.leave: Reaction equilibrium constants and conversion are Unit 7; here a reaction only reduces C.

chapters.idea: For one pure substance the equality of chemical potentials gives the vapour-pressure curve, and for a mixture it gives the bubble and dew lines of the P-x-y or T-x-y diagram.
chapters.depth: Pure component: f^L = f^V at saturation gives the vapour-pressure curve; draw the P-T diagram with triple point, critical point and the three coexistence lines. Write the Antoine equation ln P^sat = A − B/(T + C), define A, B, C, and warn that the units of P and T change with the tabulated set. Quote the Clausius-Clapeyron result d ln P^sat/d(1/T) = −Δh_vap/R (derived in Unit 4) and use it to get a latent heat from two vapour pressures. Give the Poynting correction f^L(P) = f^L(P^sat) exp[V^L(P − P^sat)/RT], with V^L the liquid molar volume in m³/mol. Mixtures: apply f_i^V = f_i^L component by component to get the P-x-y diagram (two branches at fixed T) and the T-x-y diagram (two branches at fixed P). Define bubble point (first bubble of vapour), dew point (first drop of liquid), tie line and the lever rule for phase amounts. Show an azeotrope as the point where the branches touch and x = y. Keep the mixture equations free of γ; the activity coefficient arrives in 6.4.

figure.title: P-x-y diagram at 373.15 K
figure.aria: Bubble-pressure and dew-pressure curves of benzene-toluene at 373.15 K; the bubble curve is a straight line and the dew curve bends below it, and the two meet only at the pure ends.

chapters.example: Benzene(1)–toluene(2) at 373.15 K has P₁^sat = 180.1 kPa and P₂^sat = 74.2 kPa. (a) For a liquid with x₁ = 0.30, find the bubble pressure and the vapour composition. (b) For a vapour with y₁ = 0.30, find the dew pressure and the liquid composition.
chapters.trap: Swapping x and y when reading a P-x-y diagram, and using Antoine constants without checking whether T is in K or °C and P in mmHg or bar.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 (PVT behaviour, equations of state) and Unit 4 (Clausius-Clapeyron).
chapters.leave: The derivation of Clausius-Clapeyron and residual properties stay in Unit 4; the activity-coefficient form of these equations is 6.4.

chapters.idea: An ideal solution obeys y_i P = x_i P_i^sat (Raoult's law), and a real solution needs one correction: y_i P = x_i γ_i P_i^sat.
chapters.depth: Derive Raoult's law from f_i^V = f_i^L with three assumptions: ideal-gas vapour (φ_i^V = 1), liquid standard state = pure liquid at the same T and P, and negligible Poynting correction. Then the modified form y_i P = x_i γ_i P_i^sat, where γ_i is the activity coefficient defined in Unit 5. Give the bubble-pressure recipe: read P_i^sat from Antoine, get γ_i from a model, compute P = Σ x_i γ_i P_i^sat, then y_i = x_i γ_i P_i^sat/P. Describe the bubble-temperature and dew-point versions in words instead of algebra. Define K_i = y_i/x_i = γ_i P_i^sat/P and relative volatility α₁₂ = (y₁/x₁)/(y₂/x₂) = γ₁P₁^sat/(γ₂P₂^sat). Show the reverse calculation — activity coefficients from measured data, γ_i = y_i P/(x_i P_i^sat) — and from a single azeotrope together with Gibbs-Duhem. State the azeotrope conditions x_i = y_i and γ₁P₁^sat = γ₂P₂^sat = P.

figure.title: Bubble-pressure calculation with modified Raoult's law
figure.aria: Order of steps in a bubble-pressure calculation: fix T and x, look up the vapour pressures, get activity coefficients from a model, add the partial pressures and divide to get y.

chapters.example: At 343 K a binary liquid has x₁ = 0.40, P₁^sat = 60.0 kPa and P₂^sat = 20.0 kPa. The one-parameter Margules model applies with ln γ₁ = A x₂² and ln γ₂ = A x₁², A = 1.20. Find the bubble pressure and y₁, and compare with ideal Raoult's law.
chapters.trap: Using Raoult's law on a pair with a known azeotrope such as ethanol–water, and evaluating γ_i at the wrong composition — γ_i depends on the whole mixture, not just on x_i.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 and 6.3, plus Unit 5 for the activity coefficient and its models.
chapters.leave: Derivations of the Margules, van Laar and Wilson equations and of excess Gibbs energy stay in Unit 5.

chapters.idea: In a very dilute solution the solute's fugacity is proportional to its own mole fraction with Henry's constant as the slope, not the pure-component vapour pressure.
chapters.depth: Define Henry's law as p_i = x_i H_i, or f_i = x_i k_i, with H_i in Pa (or bar) on the mole-fraction scale. Stress that H_i is the limiting slope of p_i against x_i as x_i → 0, and that the standard state is a hypothetical pure liquid at infinite dilution, so H_i is not P_i^sat. Show the link γ_i^∞ = H_i/P_i^sat and the one-parameter Margules form p₁ = x₁ exp[A(1 − x₁)²] P₁^sat with A = ln(H₁/P₁^sat). Give the temperature dependence d ln H/dT = (h̄_i^V − h̄_i^∞)/RT²: for most gases in water H rises with T, so warm soda goes flat. Give the pressure effect d ln H/dP = V̄_i^∞/RT. Extend to a dilute binary: the solute follows Henry and the solvent follows Raoult, which is what makes the two-standard-state convention work. State the practical range, roughly x_i below 0.02 to 0.05, and use dissolved oxygen in boiler feed water, CO₂ in soft drinks and oxygen in blood as examples.

figure.title: Henry's law as the dilute limit of a real solution
figure.aria: Partial pressure of component 1 against x₁: the real curve starts with the steep Henry straight line, crosses the Raoult line, and reaches the pure vapour pressure of 60 kPa at x₁ = 1.

chapters.example: Carbon dioxide in water at 298 K has a Henry constant of about 1.6 × 10³ bar on the mole-fraction scale. A soft drink is carbonated at a CO₂ partial pressure of 3.0 bar. Find the mole fraction of dissolved CO₂, and its molality in water.
chapters.trap: Reaching for P_i^sat for a gas held above its critical temperature, where no vapour pressure exists, and treating H as dimensionless — on the mole-fraction scale it carries pressure units.
chapters.prereq: 6.3 and 6.4 for the standard states and the ideal-solution limit.
chapters.leave: Multicomponent gas solubility, electrolyte solutions and salting-out are outside this book.

chapters.idea: At high pressure both phases are non-ideal, so the same fugacity equality is written with fugacity coefficients from one equation of state: y_i φ_i^V = x_i φ_i^L.
chapters.depth: Show first where modified Raoult's law breaks: φ_i^V is no longer 1, the liquid standard state and its Poynting correction become unreliable, and near the critical point the two phases are too similar for an activity coefficient model to carry the load. Write K_i = φ_i^L/φ_i^V and get both coefficients from one equation of state (van der Waals, Redlich-Kwong or Peng-Robinson, from Unit 2) with a mixing rule such as a = ΣΣ x_i x_j a_ij and b = Σ x_i b_i. Lay out the flash loop: Wilson K-value estimate, Rachford-Rice to get the vapour fraction β, EOS to get φ for both phases, update K, repeat. Name the bubble-point and dew-point versions, and note that the detailed convergence proof is taught by only a few universities. Mention retrograde condensation (a dew point crossed twice), gas-gas equilibrium, and the uses: natural gas and NGL recovery, high-pressure absorption, supercritical CO₂ extraction of spices.

figure.title: Phi-phi flash loop for high-pressure VLE
figure.aria: Iteration loop of a high-pressure flash: initial K-values, Rachford-Rice for the vapour fraction, fugacity coefficients from an equation of state, new K-values, and a return to Rachford-Rice until K stops changing.

chapters.example: At 400 K and 40 bar a two-phase mixture has x₁ = 0.25. The equation of state gives φ₁^L = 0.52, φ₁^V = 0.88, φ₂^L = 0.95 and φ₂^V = 0.97. Find K₁, K₂ and the sum x₁K₁ + x₂K₂, and say what that sum means.
chapters.trap: Carrying an ideal-gas vapour assumption to 50 bar, and using two different equations of state for the two phases, which quietly destroys the equality being solved.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 and 6.4, plus Unit 2 for cubic equations of state and their mixing rules.
chapters.leave: Detailed EOS algebra and generalized compressibility charts stay in Unit 2; three-phase high-pressure algorithms are outside this book.

chapters.idea: The same fugacity equality applied to two liquid phases gives extraction tie lines, and applied to a solid plus a solution gives the solubility curve.
chapters.depth: Liquid-liquid: for phases α and β, x_i^α γ_i^α = x_i^β γ_i^β with the same pure-liquid standard state. Explain that only the ratio γ_i^α/γ_i^β comes out of tie-line data, so a model plus Gibbs-Duhem is needed to split it; draw the binodal curve, tie lines, the plait point of a ternary, and the distribution coefficient K_D = x_i^β/x_i^α used for solvent extraction. Add a short paragraph on vapour-liquid-liquid equilibrium: three phases need f_i^L1 = f_i^L2 = f_i^V and F = C − P + 2 = 1 for a binary, so the three-phase pressure at a given T is a single number. Solid-liquid: a pure solid 1 in equilibrium with a liquid gives ln(x₁γ₁) = −(Δh_fus/R)(1/T − 1/T_m), with Δh_fus in J/mol and T_m in K, assuming ΔCp ≈ 0; setting γ₁ = 1 gives the ideal solubility, which always over-predicts for a non-ideal solution. Cover the eutectic of two solids, crystallisation, and uses such as essential-oil extraction, sugar and salt crystallisation, and wax deposition in pipelines.

figure.title: Ideal solubility falling as the heat of fusion rises
figure.aria: Ideal solubility against temperature for two solids melting at 330 K; both curves meet at the melting point x₁ = 1, and the solid with the larger heat of fusion dissolves far less at any lower temperature.

chapters.example: A solid melts at 330 K with Δh_fus = 20.0 kJ/mol. (a) Find its ideal solubility (mole fraction) in a liquid at 300 K. (b) Find the real solubility if the activity coefficient of the solid in the liquid is 1.8.
chapters.trap: Dropping γ₁ in a solid-liquid calculation and then believing the high solubility obtained, and using the same standard state for both liquid phases in an LLE calculation.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 and 6.4, and Unit 5 for activity coefficients and excess Gibbs energy.
chapters.leave: Obtaining γ from excess Gibbs energy models stays in Unit 5; solid-phase polymorphism and hydrate equilibria are outside this book.
